                          Caribou: Intelligent Distributed Storage

ABSTRACT                                                                              Data movement between layers can be reduced by pushing
The ever increasing amount of data being handled in data                           operators down to storage. This is already done in shared-
centers causes an intrinsic inefficiency: moving data around                       disk architectures that rely on traditional servers to provide
is expensive in terms of bandwidth, latency, and power con-                        storage supporting query offloading [62]. Today, however,
sumption, especially given the low computational complex-                          processing offload can be achieved with much less hardware
ity of many database operations.                                                   and resources, for instance, by using SSDs embedded with
   In this paper we explore near-data processing in database                       computational capabilities [10, 14, 23, 24, 64]. Compared
engines, i.e., the option of offloading part of the compu-                         to these two approaches, we explore an alternative design
tation directly to the storage nodes. We implement our                             point: smart distributed storage with replication that ex-
ideas in Caribou, an intelligent distributed storage layer in-                     poses a high level interface such as those found in shared
corporating many of the lessons learned while building sys-                        disk DBMSs and provides performance characteristics on a
tems with specialized hardware. Caribou provides access to                         par with CPUs, but is implemented with energy efficient
DRAM/NVRAM storage over the network through a simple                               specialized hardware such as that found in “active” SSDs.
key-value store interface, with each storage node providing                           In this work we use DRAM for storage as it allows us
high-bandwidth near-data processing at line rate and fault                         to explore near-data processing ideas for upcoming memory
tolerance through replication. The result is a highly effi-                        technologies without being limited by either random access
cient, distributed, intelligent data storage that can be used                      performance or bandwidth of the underlying medium. Fur-
to both boost performance and reduce power consumption                             thermore, storage is already moving away from strict block-
and real estate usage in the data center thanks to the micro-                      based interfaces and allows more flexible access methods [6].
server architecture adopted.                                                       For instance, Intel Optane SSDs1 can be used as a persistent
                                                                                   extension of RAM, blurring the boundaries between main-
                                                                                   memory and persistent storage.

to execute scans without having to send multiple requests
to the storage. We have augmented the key-value store with
bitmap indexes for efficient scan operations.

Near-data computation: We implement selection both
for structured and unstructured data in an effort to reduce
data movement even further in a wide range of workloads.
Our design ensures that in-storage processing has no nega-
tive impact on the data retrieval rate as the selection opera-
tors are parameterizable at runtime (require no reprogram-           Figure 1: Caribou offers replicated intelligent storage
ming for different queries).                                         for shared-data databases. Replication uses Zookeeper’s
                                                                     Atomic Broadcast and is transparent to the layers above.
Fault tolerance through transparent replication: We
demonstrated in earlier work [21] that FPGAs can be used
to build replication into a system at high throughput and            3.    SYSTEM OVERVIEW
without slowing down common operations. In this work we
integrate this module into a complex processing pipeline.            3.1    Interface

   For relational database use-cases, it is beneficial if the
storage nodes can differentiate between data belonging to
one table, a set of tables, and others. This way, the cost
of scan operations, for instance, are not influenced by the
size of other tables. The allocator module has support for
tablespaces but, in our experiments, by default a single ta-
blespace is used given that the prototype platform has less
DRAM than a real system would. A tablespace is defined as
a set of keys that belong to the same logical collection and
is encoded in the high order bits of the key. They are imple-
